extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning set theory / introductory proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter material defining and comparing cardinalities of sets, including bijections, countable vs uncountable sets, Cantor's diagonal argument, and basic closure results (products, unions). Aimed to teach how to prove two sets have the same or different cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of cardinalities (Definition 13.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: |A| = |B| if and only if there exists a bijection f : A → B; if no such bijection exists then |A| ≠ |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to finite and infinite sets. To show two sets have equal cardinality it suffices to find one bijection between them. Examples: f(n) = −n shows |A| = |B| in Example 13.1; explicit table/bijection exhibits |N| = |Z| in Example 13.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: bijection, injection, surjection
rubrics_metrics.description: A bijective function is called a bijection. An injective function is an injection; a surjective function is a surjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bijections are central, these terms are used interchangeably with 'bijective function', etc. The text emphasizes that finding any one bijection is enough to conclude equality of cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of bijection N → Z (Theorem 13.1 / Example 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an explicit bijection f : N → Z (shown by an alternating table), hence |N| = |Z|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table lists integers in an order so every integer appears exactly once; the construction is both injective and surjective. The example demonstrates how infinite sets can have unintuitive equalities of size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's diagonal argument (non-surjectivity N → R) / Theorem 13.2
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no surjective functions f : N → R (hence no bijections), so |N| ≠ |R|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a real number b whose nth decimal digit differs from the nth digit of f(n) (choose e.g. 6 when digit ≠6, else 2) to guarantee b ≠ f(n) for every n. This diagonal construction works for any purported enumeration f and proves non-surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of countably infinite and uncountable (Definition 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if |N| = |A| (i.e., there exists a bijection f : N → A). A set A is uncountable if A is infinite and there exists no bijection f : N → A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus Z and other sets with bijections to N are countably infinite; R is uncountable. Countably infinite sets can be 'listed' as an infinite sequence f(1), f(2), ....

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation aleph-naught (Definition 13.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cardinality of the natural numbers is denoted |N| = ℵ0 (aleph-naught).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any countably infinite set has cardinality ℵ0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of countably infinite sets (Theorem 13.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if and only if its elements can be arranged in an infinite list a1, a2, a3, ... (i.e., there is a bijection f : N → A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove a set is countable it suffices to produce such a list; conversely, a list yields a bijection. This is used to show sets like primes are countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q is countable (Theorem 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set Q of rational numbers is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: arrange rationals in a two-dimensional array (columns by numerator, reduced fractions) and follow a snaking (diagonal-type) path through the array to list every rational exactly once; avoid duplicates by using reduced forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product of two countable sets is countable (Theorem 13.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are both countably infinite, then A × B is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write A and B as lists and draw an infinite path through the grid A×B (diagonal/snaking) to enumerate all ordered pairs; used to deduce Q×Q countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite product / induction corollary (Corollary 13.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n countably infinite sets A1,...,An (n ≥ 2), the Cartesian product A1 × A2 × ... × An is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction using Theorem 13.5: product of two countables is countable, then extend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of two countable sets is countable (Theorem 13.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countably infinite, then A ∪ B is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave the lists for A and B: A ∪ B = {a1, b1, a2, b2, ...}, omitting duplicates. This gives a list/bijection from N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing cardinalities |A| < |B| (Definition 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: |A| = |B| means there is a bijection A → B. |A| < |B| means there exists an injective function f : A → B but no surjective function A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For finite sets this matches usual notion of 'fewer elements'. For infinite sets, exhibit an injection and argue impossibility of a surjection (e.g., identity injection N → R shows |N| ≤ |R| but diagonalization shows no surjection, so |N| < |R|).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict inequality to power set (Cantor's theorem, Theorem 13.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, |A| < |P(A)| (the power set has strictly larger cardinality than A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: injection x ↦ {x} shows |A| ≤ |P(A)|. Assume a surjection f : A → P(A); define B = { x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x) } and derive contradiction whether the preimage a of B belongs to B or not (diagonal/Russell-style argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite ascending chain of cardinalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting with N, one obtains K = |N| < |P(N)| < |P(P(N))| < ... , an infinite sequence of strictly increasing cardinalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated application of Cantor's theorem yields ever larger infinities. The text also remarks (without proof) that |R| = |P(N)|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability preserved by infinite subset of a countable set (Theorem 13.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an infinite subset of a countably infinite set B, then A is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: traverse the list for B and select elements belonging to A to form an infinite list for A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncountability preserved by supersets (Theorem 13.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U ⊆ A and U is uncountable, then A is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if A were countable, then infinite subset U of countable A would be countable (Theorem 13.8), contradicting U uncountable. Useful for showing larger spaces like R^2 are uncountable because they contain R as subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques to show countability or uncountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main methods: (1) To show A is countable, provide a bijection f : N → A or give an explicit infinite listing of elements; (2) To show A is uncountable, show no surjection N → A exists, often via Cantor's diagonalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: listing (snake/diagonal enumeration) for Q; diagonal construction for R. Also useful: show injection into or from known (un)countable sets and apply Theorems 13.8/13.9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example bijection constructions (illustrative rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete bijections used in examples: f(n)=−n mapping A={n∈Z:...} to another; f(n)=2n maps Z to even integers; explicit table enumerations for N→Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These serve as models for constructing bijections in exercises (provide a formula rather than just a table where requested). The exercises ask to describe bijections with formulas.
